title: Saw
full_review:
On the surface, "Saw" (Lions Gate), a new horror thriller directed by James Wan, appears to be nothing more than a gory exercise in depravity devoid of any redeeming moral value. But if you look past its severed limbs and shock-value story line, you realize that's exactly what it is.

The setup is simple. Two apparent strangers -- an unhappily married surgeon, Dr. Lawrence Gordon (Cary Elwes), and an angry young shutterbug named Adam (Leigh Whannell, who also wrote the screenplay) -- awake to find themselves chained and shackled in a squalid subterranean chamber.

Neither man knows why he has been abducted. On the floor between them is a third man, shot in the head and lying in a pool of his own blood, his limp hands clutching a gun and a small tape recorder.

Gordon finds an audiocassette planted in his pocket which contains an ultimatum from their jailer: Either Gordon kills Adam within an allotted time frame or their shadowy captor -- who monitors their actions via hidden video cameras -- will leave them both to die, and, as added incentive, will also kill Gordon's wife (Monica Potter) and young daughter (Makenzie Vega).
Gordon tells Adam that he believes that the madman behind their puzzling predicament may be the same psychopath responsible for a series of equally macabre abductions: a deranged mastermind known only as "Jigsaw." Gordon reveals that he himself had been questioned by the police as a suspect.

All of Jigsaw's victims are "morally wayward" people, who are trying to hide some dirty little secret like drug addiction or, in Gordon's case, marital infidelity. Obsessed with teaching his prey the value of life, Jigsaw has devised grisly games which they must play in order to survive -- sort of a serial killer's version of self-help therapy. Faced with impossible choices they must struggle to win back their life or die trying.

Shown in gruesome flashbacks, past contestants on "Wheel of Torture" include a man who must save himself from being buried alive by crawling through a gauntlet of razor wire, and a female junkie forced to disembowel a man in order to prevent a steel, bear-trap-like gizmo affixed to her head from mangling her face.
Danny Glover plays a police detective obsessed with tracking down the killer.

The setup is actually quite intriguing. But any hopes of Hitchcockian suspense are soon dashed by a stomach-churning barrage of stylized sadism parading as entertainment.

Full of creepy atmospherics a la David Fincher's "Seven," the story nosedives from lurid to laughable in the final reel and is capped off with a ridiculous shaggy-dog ending that tries -- unsuccessfully -- to mimic the final gasp-inducing revelation of Bryan Singer's "The Usual Suspects."

All in all, "Saw" is the most recent example of packaging venality as a way to sell tickets.

Throughout much of his ordeal, Gordon remains calm, his eyes scanning the room for any possible escape; moviegoers may find themselves doing the same. "Saw" is best left unseen.

Due to much graphic violence and recurring rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
